To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we were able to measure the local depolarization effects in a polarized 14 NH 4 F target by hitting it with a 1.2 GeV electron beam.
the polarized 14NH3 target chips can survive the electron beam intensity of 70 nA at 1.2 GeV and that the target temperature can be kept below 10 K by a suitable design of the cooling system.
the polarization loss of the target is not caused by heating, but by radiation damage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the polarized 14 NH 4 Br target in an intense electron (1.2 Gev) beam.
the study of the behaviour of polarized 14 NH 4 Br target material in an intense electron or positron beam.
the investigation of the behaviour of polarized 14 NH 4 Cl target material at an electron beam spot of 1.2 GeV.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence for any local depolarization effects at the beam spot of an electron beam with an intensity of about 70 nA.
the heating of the target material due to the electron beam is not the dominant effect which leads to depolarization.
the target chips are not damaged and the target material is not destroyed by the beam heating up to the maximum beam intensities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the heating effects are negligible.
we have shown that the polarized target can be operated at an intensity of 50 nA with no observable damage.
the polarized target material is stable against the electron beam up to 70 nA and the polarization is not reduced.
The main takeaway from our work is that
at a beam energy of 1.2 GeV the local target heating by a 70 nA electron beam is about 2.3 K, which is much lower than the critical temperature of 3.2 K of the superconducting magnet.
